newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Mixed reaction to RBNZ currency assumption.
newsitem.headline: Mixed reaction to RBNZ currency assumption.

text.p: Dealers and economists gave mixed reviews on Friday to the Reserve Bank of New Zealand's altered currency assumption in its latest economic projections.
The Reserve Bank said inflation forecasts in its statement assumed the trade-weighted nominal exchange rate to remain constant around 65.0 throughout its forecast period.

In its last major statement in June, the bank had assumed the average value of the Trade-Weighted Index (TWI) to rise 1.7 percent annually to reach 66.7 by March 1999 from a starting point of 64.0 in the September 1996 quarter.

The bank pointed out that the new TWI assumption was the main factor behind a revision in its 1998/99 inflation forecasts. It now sees underlying inflation falling to an annual 0.5 percent by March 1999, where before it saw negative inflation of 0.4 percent at that time.

"I'd also say that it's possibly another means by which they're trying to emphasise the mix in monetary conditions, keeping the emphasis on interest rates and reducing the emphasis on the exchange rate," said ANZ Chief Economist Paul Stewart.

Reserve Bank Governor Don Brash has stressed in the past that the bank cannot control the mix of monetary conditions but that it might have preferred earlier tightening to occur more through interest rates than the currency.
Doyle Paterson Brown economist Stephen Toplis said the bank was trying to refocus people's minds on the mix of the currency and interest rates within overall monetary conditions.
He said the bank, by assuming flat interest rates at 10 percent and a flat nominal exchange rate, was telling the markets: "You work it out for yourself."
Some dealers questioned the logic of the assumptions.
"We've got the highest real yields in the OECD but we're assuming a non-appreciating currency, which I think is illogical," an Auckland forex trader said.

"We feel that they are trying to create a situation that is pretty impossible. Keep the TWI down, keep the exchange rate down but keep rates high...it does not really make sense," said a Wellington trader.

Bank of New Zealand economist Tony Alexander said the new TWI assumption was the biggest surprise in the statement, which said any easing was "off the agenda" pending conclusive evidence that inflation would fall away sharply in 1997 and beyond.

"They say they've made it there so that further out the underlying inflation projection remains within the 0-2 percent band, but I think more especially they've had to do it because if they'd retained the old assumption they would have had a much sharper fall in underlying inflation over the next 12 to 18 months and would, I think, have been encouraging the market implicitly to take interest rates down," he said.

"I continue to believe their greatest source of concern is about the stimulatory impact of interest rates, and so I just think they've come up with a method of keeping the interest rates high without making it sound like they're tightening
policy, and they've just used this exchange rate assumption to do that."

Bancorp Treasury Services said in a commentary that the flat TWI assumption meant the RBNZ saw exchange rates currently having little or no effect on inflation outcomes. "In the end this is a less complicated method and an improvement," it said.
Most dealers were high skeptical of the bank's ability to change the weighting of the exchange and interest rates in setting monetary conditions.
"They want an easing through the currency but you can't do it. It won't work," said the chief dealer of a Wellington bank.
"As soon as they project 90-day bills to hang around 10 percent then the currency goes up," he said. "The Japanese and euros will continue to come in."
-- Wellington newsroom 64 4 4734 746
